summary: The machine has the runtime and DocumentDB MCP data-plane tools needed to build the Node.js LangChain multi-agent sample (Node 24, npx, documentdb MCP server, Azure CLI, Learn docs server, many DocumentDB agent skills). Key service facts from the cold answers were partially or fully incorrect in places (resource type, CLI group, Bicep/Terraform resource, connection-string form, billing model, vector-index syntax, built-in text/vector search vs external search, local gateway port). Those facts are verifiable from Microsoft Learn and the installed DocumentDB skills; the build can start but the builder must apply the corrections below and a few conveniences (mongosh) are not installed.
summary_points: All essential build tools for the sample are present: Node.js (v24), npm/npx, documentdb MCP server (data-plane), azure MCP server, and Microsoft Learn search; the documentdb agent skills are installed and usable.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated: the current managed resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts); az documentdb mongocluster ... is the CLI group; Bicep/Terraform resource is mongoClusters; DocumentDB uses vCore/compute tiers (M-series) not RUs; the cluster provides its own connection string shape (SRV/global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and supports native SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) modes.

Vector-search/index syntax is DocumentDB-specific (createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions and kinds vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann) — the cold 'knn' index spec used by some other engines is not correct here.
Local development: a DocumentDB local gateway image and gateway port 10260 are provided for local runs; using mongo:6.0:27017 is a fall-back but not the DocumentDB local developer experience.
Missing conveniences (mongosh CLI) and a small number of unverified sample-level choices (document schema, embedding dims to use) remain and should be resolved by the builder before committing code.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. (Sub-resources for MongoDB-style resources are modeled under the database account.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The modern managed MongoDB-compatible cluster resource uses the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider but the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string for the Azure service: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account-name>@ . The scheme is mongodb:// (or mongodb+srv:// if SRV is available), host suffix is <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, default port 10255 for TLS. Options must include SSL/TLS enabled (ssl=true or tls=true) and retryWrites=false for Cosmos-style MongoDB endpoints.
confusions.grounded_answer: This cold answer describes the legacy Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection string. For current Azure DocumentDB vCore mongoClusters the connection string format differs: the cluster provides SCRAM and SRV forms such as mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster-name>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/... (or explicit hosts returned by az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings). Do not assume the cosmos.azure.com account host suffix nor port 10255 for the vCore mongoCluster; use the connection strings returned by az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal.

grounding_links.title: Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString-Description

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflates Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API connection string shape (account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) with the modern DocumentDB vCore cluster connection strings (mongocluster.global.* / SRV). Both expose MongoDB wire protocol but use different host suffixes and service-specific formats.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: There are multiple billing models: the classic model is RU/s (Request Units) provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale) and also serverless accounts for low-volume use. In addition, Azure offers vCore/dedicated-cluster style MongoDB-compatible SKUs (M-series instance sizes such as M30 etc.) for dedicated compute — those are billed as instance sizes rather than pure RUs. Choose RUs/Autoscale for Cosmos-style accounts or a vCore-style dedicated cluster SKU when you need dedicated MongoDB cluster characteristics.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (the vCore MongoDB-compatible service) the billing model is compute (cluster tier: M-series / vCores) and storage; there are no RUs. Azure DocumentDB is charged by cluster tier (vCores) and storage; RUs refer to Cosmos DB RU-based accounts (a different product).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (pricing)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer combined both RU-based Cosmos DB models and the vCore M-series model; Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers and storage, not request units.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU/s model docs (confusingly similar naming)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based autoscale or uses Cosmos-specific throughput APIs when creating or sizing clusters and indexes, this will not match the vCore DocumentDB billing model and could lead to incorrect sizing/assumptions.
improvements: Add a clear distinction in the top-level product overview pages: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses M-series compute tiers; Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB uses RUs' so migration and sample docs don't conflate the two.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary authentication is MongoDB-style user/password (SCRAM) using database users managed on the account (or the account primary keys). The service also exposes account keys (primary/secondary keys) and resource tokens for fine-grained access. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integration is not the default MongoDB auth path; where supported you obtain an AAD access token from the Microsoft identity platform and exchange it according to the service docs — typically the driver still connects with the standard MongoDB connection string and credentials (username/password) and AAD is used for control-plane / RBAC in the Azure portal. In practice for the Node.js MongoDB driver you will most commonly supply the connection string credentials; if AAD is required you must acquire an access token and follow the provider's instructions to supply it as the driver credential (this is a non-standard flow and varies by service API/version).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters support NativeAuth (SCRAM username/password) by default and also an explicit Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) mode. When Microsoft Entra ID auth is enabled on the cluster you obtain an Entra-issued OIDC access token and present it to the driver via the driver’s OIDC/token callback mechanism; the product docs show how to enable MicrosoftEntraID and how to configure token callbacks in Node.js.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
AuthenticationMode type (NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer understated the first-class support for Microsoft Entra ID on vCore clusters; Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC) is an explicit, supported mode and there are documented driver integration patterns.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is impossible or only used for control-plane tasks, they would miss the documented token-callback pattern and may not implement recommended authentication for managed identities or service principals.
improvements: Clarify examples in quickstarts showing both: (a) the common SCRAM connection via DOCUMENTDB_URI (env var) and (b) the Entra ID token-callback pattern (DefaultAzureCredential + driver OIDC callback) with a short, copyable Node.js snippet.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For MongoDB-compatible workloads use the official MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the mongodb npm package / MongoClient). There is an Azure SDK for Cosmos DB, but for the MongoDB API you should use the standard MongoDB driver to talk to the cluster; no special service-specific client is required for application data-plane operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (npm 'mongodb' for Node.js). Quickstarts and the product docs advise using the MongoDB driver and show Node.js examples using MongoClient and environment-supplied connection strings.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: The service supports vector indexes (vendor-provided implementations such as HNSW, IVF or DiskANN on managed clusters depending on SKU). The index is created via a MongoDB createIndex command on the embedding field. Example (Mongo shell-like): db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'knn' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — parameter names vary by service version, but the general form is createIndex with a knn/vector index spec and a knnVector/options object specifying dimensions and algorithm.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes: vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann (with product quantization and half-precision options). The index is created via a createIndexes/db.runCommand payload that uses a 'cosmosSearch' index spec (e.g., createIndexes with key { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-ivf' | 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-diskann', dimensions: <n>, ... }). The syntax is DocumentDB-specific rather than a generic 'knnVector' option.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use vector search with Node.js in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a 'knn'/'knnVector' spec common in other vector-enabled MongoDB variants; DocumentDB uses its own 'cosmosSearch' index creation spec and 'cosmosSearchOptions' parameters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder generates the wrong createIndex payload (knnVector style), index creation will fail and vector search will not be usable. The sample must create vector indexes using the DocumentDB createIndexes payload with cosmosSearchOptions.
improvements: Provide a short example index-creation JSON in the documentdb-vector-search skill and include it in quickstarts for Node.js (exact property names and kinds).
Include an example runCommand/createIndexes snippet in the sample seed script so builders don't invent incompatible index syntax.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search is typically implemented by integrating Cosmos/DocumentDB with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or by using the service's built-in text indexing if the API exposes it. Hybrid search (text + vector) is normally performed at the application layer or by using an index that supports combined scoring (if the managed vector index supports predicates/metadata filtering). In many setups you run a vector nearest-neighbor query to get candidates and then apply a text-based ranking/filtering pass (or use Azure Cognitive Search's combined capabilities if you sync data there).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text and vector search that you invoke via the $search aggregation stage and the 'cosmosSearch' operator. You can create search indexes (createSearchIndexes / createIndexes with 'text' or 'cosmosSearch' options) and do hybrid (lexical + vector) retrieval via the same $search stage (cosmosSearch supports vector and text operators and pre-filtering), so you do not need Azure Cognitive Search for many use cases.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (text + vector search, cosmosSearch operator)
Full text (createSearchIndexes) and $search aggregation stage

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumes an external Azure Cognitive Search integration (common for Cosmos DB Core/NoSQL scenarios) rather than the DocumentDB product's integrated text and vector search capability.

confusions.build_risk: If the builder creates an external Azure Cognitive Search pipeline, they add unnecessary complexity and cost; the sample can be simpler by using the built-in $search/cosmosSearch pipeline.
improvements: Document in quickstarts that $search + cosmosSearch supports combined vector and lexical retrieval and show a minimal hybrid example (vector + text boosting) in the documentdb-vector-search skill and sample app.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Support is versioned by account and can vary; historically Azure's MongoDB-compatible service has announced compatibility with MongoDB wire protocol versions corresponding to 4.x and later 5.x/6.x in progressive releases (some managed clusters support 6.0 or 7.0 protocol in newer SKUs). Not all native MongoDB server features are supported — things commonly missing or limited include server-side JavaScript, some rarely used aggregation stages and expressions, certain admin commands, and behavior differences in transactions and change streams depending on the deployment type. Always check the account's reported supported wire version and test critical MongoDB features against the live cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0 (current service documentation enumerates 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0) and advertises ~99% operator compatibility; a small set of admin commands or rarely used operators may be unsupported. Builders should consult the MongoDB compatibility and feature-compatibility pages and run the provided compatibility assessment before migration.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions supported)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was imprecise and conservative; the service now documents explicit supported wire protocol versions (5.0–8.0).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes older wire versions or omits checking compatibility for a needed feature (e.g., change streams or a specific aggregation stage), they may hit runtime incompatibilities.
improvements: Add a single 'Supported wire versions' callout to the quickstart and the agent-kit skills showing which MongoDB versions are supported (5.0-8.0) and link to the compatibility assessment tool.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For MongoDB-compatible development you typically run the official MongoDB Docker image (for example mongo:6.0) locally and connect on port 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists but historically only supports the Core (SQL) API and not the MongoDB API; therefore it is not a drop-in for MongoDB API development. Use a local MongoDB server (docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:6.0) for local tests.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an official local gateway Docker image for DocumentDB development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and the gateway listens on port 10260 by default; use that image and port for a faithful DocumentDB local dev experience. Using a plain mongo:6.0 container is a possible fallback but does not emulate DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, search operators, DocumentDB auth variants, etc.).

grounding_links.title: Run DocumentDB locally (gateway image and port 10260)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested the generic mongo image and port 27017 (useful for generic MongoDB app testing) but the DocumentDB local developer experience uses the project gateway image and port 10260 to better match the managed service behavior.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder relies on a plain mongo:6.0 local image for integration tests they may miss DocumentDB-specific behaviors (index creation semantics, vector-search operator names, OIDC token callback differences).
improvements: Add a small local-dev snippet in the documentdb-local-deployment skill showing the exact docker run line for the DocumentDB gateway (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and port 10260.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change-like functionality is available but varies: Cosmos DB has its Change Feed (a different mechanism than MongoDB change streams) which is always available for Core API and exposed via SDKs. MongoDB-style change streams are supported in some MongoDB-compatible account versions but may be limited depending on account SKU and wire version; in many cases you either use the service's Change Feed or you enable a specific compatibility/server version that supports change streams. Verify and enable change-stream support per-account if you require MongoDB change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams and includes features like multishard change streams (preview) and configurable pre-images/updateDescription settings; some change-stream features must be enabled (multi-shard change streams feature, enabling pre-images, etc.). The product docs show how to enable the feature and the portal/ARM properties to change.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams: enable multi-shard change streams (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated Cosmos DB Core change feed patterns with DocumentDB's documented MongoDB-style change streams and did not call out the documented enablement steps (e.g., enabling multishard change stream feature).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects change streams to be available without enabling cluster features, they may get no events or incomplete behavior; sample should document any feature toggles required.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Enable change streams' step in the sample README and the documentdb-mcp-setup skill when the sample uses change streams, linking to the portal/az CLI/ARM commands that toggle the feature.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service-specific MCP server profile for DocumentDB (the environment refers to a 'documentdb' MCP server). The general Azure MCP server may cover control-plane (resource management) operations, but for data-plane inspection and index/query-plan tooling you should use the documentdb-specific MCP server/tools that are wired to the cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, aggregate, etc.). The azure MCP server provides control-plane and complementary docs/tools; both are useful but data-plane inspection best comes from the documentdb MCP server.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name DocumentDB for its original document database service; that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB as the multi-model global service. Today 'DocumentDB' is often used interchangeably in legacy docs. Azure Cosmos DB is the managed global service; the open-source 'documentdb' projects (client SDKs and early prototypes) were related to the original DocumentDB SDKs but are separate from the cloud service. In short: DocumentDB was the original name / concept that became Cosmos DB; Azure Cosmos DB provides multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is essentially correct but nuanced: Azure DocumentDB (the current vCore MongoDB-compatible offering) was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' in older messaging; the open-source DocumentDB engine is the engine powering Azure DocumentDB and is an independent open-source project. Azure Cosmos DB (RU-style) and Azure DocumentDB (vCore, mongoClusters) are separate services now.

grounding_links.title: Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (relation to Cosmos DB and open-source DocumentDB)

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine for the MongoDB-compatible endpoint is the service's managed implementation that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol (it is not literally a stock MongoDB server in all SKUs). That means most MongoDB drivers work unchanged, but there are subtle behavioral differences and feature gaps (e.g., some aggregation stages, admin commands, or storage-layer semantics). Test and validate features (transactions, change streams, advanced aggregation) against the target cluster and prefer the official MongoDB driver for data-plane operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and more specific: Azure DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine (available on GitHub), which is implemented on top of PostgreSQL extensions for BSON and vector support; nevertheless the service speaks the MongoDB wire protocol and most drivers and tools work unchanged — but there are documented small feature gaps and admin command differences to test.

confusions.question: What database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_fintech_18 for all collections and operations in this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: the run environment (skill_md) explicitly instructs to use database sample_fintech_18 for this sample.

confusions.question: Which collections and indexes will the sample create for the multi-agent chargeback flow?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: transactions, communications, disputes, decisions. Indexes: standard indexes on transactionId, userId, timestamp. A vector index on transactions.embedding for evidence retrieval (createIndex({ embedding: 'knn' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw' } })). Also create text indexes on communications.message for keyword search (db.communications.createIndex({ message: 'text' })).
confusions.grounded_answer: The prompt does not specify exact collection names, field names or vector-dimensions; the DocumentDB vector-index syntax must use the DocumentDB createIndexes format with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann), and text indexes are created using the service's text search index commands (createSearchIndexes/createIndexes), but the precise scheme (collection names and embedding dimension) is a builder decision not covered by docs.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The sample prompt left collection names and index parameters unspecified; the cold answer invented names and a 1536-dimension assumption (tied to a particular embedding model) that no installed skill/doc confirmed.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder relies on a hard-coded embedding dimension (1536) but uses a different embedding model in the sample, vector queries/indexes will mismatch and search will fail or produce poor results.
improvements: Document in the sample README which embedding model is assumed (and its output dimension) and provide a variable in .env.example to set embedding dim for index creation.
Make the seed-and-index script parameterized so builders can choose vector dimensions and index kind (ivf/hnsw/diskann) at runtime.

confusions.question: How will the Node.js app connect to the cluster in code?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to the official MongoDB Node.js driver: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); Do not hard-code credentials—use the provided URI at runtime.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Quickstarts and the run environment instruct reading the cluster connection string from an env var (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and instantiating MongoClient. The documentdb-driver skill also recommends a singleton MongoClient pattern.

confusions.question: What authentication method will the sample use at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will use the credentials embedded in the DOCUMENTDB_URI (standard MongoDB username/password / SCRAM). We will not attempt an AAD OAuth flow in this sample; the driver authenticates using the connection string supplied in DOCUMENTDB_URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and consistent with the run environment: use the connection-string credentials (SCRAM) read from DOCUMENTDB_URI by default; document shows how to enable Microsoft Entra ID but the sample can default to SCRAM for simplicity.

confusions.question: Which tool will the build use to inspect collections, indexes and query plans as required by the run environment?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the provided documentdb MCP server connection profile named 'default' and its tooling to inspect collections, indexes and query plans. For ad-hoc checks use the MongoDB shell or MongoDB Compass pointed at DOCUMENTDB_URI to validate collections and indexes created by the sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the inventory includes a documentdb MCP server with tools (list_databases, list_indexes, explain_operation, aggregate). The az CLI and portal are complementary; mongosh/Compass are optional ad-hoc tools (mongosh not installed here).

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and vector dimension
information_gaps.description: No installed skill, doc or prompt-supplied value fixes the embedding model (provider + model) for the sample, which determines vector dimension (e.g., 1536 vs 3072). I searched Learn docs and the prompt; the prompt review suggested using an OpenAI model by assumption but no authoritative choice exists. The builder must pick the embedding model and then create indexes with matching 'dimensions'.

information_gaps.title: Concrete sample document schema
information_gaps.description: The prompt does not specify exact collection names or field names (transactions, communications, disputes, decisions) or their exact field shapes. I checked prompt and installed skills but found no canonical schema to use; the builder must choose and document the schema and include an idempotent seed script.

information_gaps.title: Which LLM/embedding provider and model to use in sample
information_gaps.description: The prompt review asked which AI provider and exact models should be used (this affects index dims and API keys). No skill or doc in the inventory picks provider/model for the sample; builder must choose and document it (e.g., OpenAI embeddings text-embedding-3-small, gpt-4o-mini for reasoning).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the ARM/Bicep/Terraform resource type (not databaseAccounts).
Use az documentdb mongocluster ... CLI commands to inspect or manage the vCore cluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings) rather than az cosmosdb.

Create vector indexes using the DocumentDB 'createIndexes' payload and 'cosmosSearchOptions' (kind: vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann) and match the 'dimensions' to the chosen embedding model.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the run environment forbids provisioning a new cluster. If future provisioning/IaC is needed, install Azure Developer CLI via its official installer.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (no provisioning). If IaC is desired later, install bicep CLI (az bicep install) or use az deployment with Bicep files.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample. If Terraform-based deployment is needed later, install Terraform and the AzAPI provider or use Azure Verified Modules.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the Node.js sample. Add if you later need to build .NET functions or bindings.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Worth adding for convenient local interactive debugging and ad-hoc checks of collections/indexes. Install mongosh (MongoDB Shell) from MongoDB downloads or via package manager. Workaround: use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_sample_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation) or MongoDB Compass connected to the cluster.
